title: Organic Chemistry: Naming, Isomers and Polymers

standard_text: Homologous series and functional groups (alkanes, alkenes, alcohols, carboxylic acids, esters, amines, amides); IUPAC naming; structural isomers; physical properties and intermolecular forces; addition, substitution and oxidation reactions; addition and condensation polymers. (Senior Secondary Chemistry, Unit 4: Structure, synthesis and design)

body_html:
How to think about it

Organic compounds are grouped into homologous series with the same functional group: alkanes (C–C), alkenes (C=C), alcohols (–OH), carboxylic acids (–COOH), esters (–COO–), amines (–NH₂). IUPAC names give the longest chain, the position of the functional group and any branches.

Alkenes undergo addition; alkanes undergo substitution; primary alcohols oxidise to carboxylic acids. Alkenes join into addition polymers; monomers with two functional groups form condensation polymers such as polyesters and proteins.

Example

Name CH₃CH₂CH₂OH

3 carbons: prop-

OH on carbon 1

Answer: propan-1-ol

Example

Molecular formula of the alkane with 5 carbons?

CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, n = 5

Answer: C₅H₁₂

Common mistakes

  • Numbering the chain from the wrong end.
  • Thinking isomers must have the same structure.
  • Saying polymerisation of ethene releases water.

faq.q: Why do short-chain alcohols dissolve in water but alkanes do not?
faq.a: The –OH group forms hydrogen bonds with water; alkanes are non-polar and cannot.

faq.q: What is the difference between addition and condensation polymers?
faq.a: Addition polymers form from alkenes with no other product; condensation polymers form from monomers with two functional groups and release a small molecule such as water.

items.q: What is a condensation polymer?

a polymer made when monomers join and release a small molecule such as water
items.e: Polyesters, nylon and proteins are condensation polymers.

items.q: What is a homologous series?
c: a family of compounds with the same functional group and general formula, each differing by CH₂

items.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃COOH?

items.q: How many moles of oxygen are needed to burn one mole of C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> completely?
items.e: C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub> + (3n+1)/2 O<sub>2</sub> → nCO<sub>2</sub> + (n+1)H<sub>2</sub>O. 4 CO₂ need 8 O atoms, 5 H₂O need 5 O atoms: 13 ÷ 2 = 6½.

items.q: Why do alcohols have higher boiling points than alkanes of similar mass?
